items.readable_text:
Content:
We know how to solve a system of differential equations when they're decoupled. However, most systems are not decoupled. So, how do we solve them?

Content:
Let's consider a general linear system of two differential equations:

Content:
[MATH: {x_{1}^{′}(t) = ax_{1}(t) + bx_{2}(t); x_{2}^{′}(t) = cx_{1}(t) + dx_{2}(t)]

Content:
It turns out that if the matrix [MATH: A] has two distinct real eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2], then [MATH: A] is diagonalizable and we can solve the system.

Content:
If the eigenvectors corresponding to [MATH: \color{red}\lambda_1] and [MATH: \color{blue}\lambda_2] are [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},] respectively, then the general solution to our original system can be written as
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
This result is true for any [MATH: n \times n] system with [MATH: n] distinct eigenvalues. We'll prove this result for a [MATH: 2\times 2] system at the end of the lesson.

Content:
Now, let's see some concrete examples.

Therefore, the general solution of our matrix differential equation is

[MATH: x(t)|= c_{1}[1; − 2]e^{− t} + c_{2}[2; 5]e^{2t}, c_{1}, c_{2} ∈ R.]

    • For [MATH: \lambda_1 =-3,] we get [MATH: [0|0; − 3|4]] So, we get an eigenvector [MATH: [4; 3]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We know how to solve a system of differential equations when they're decoupled. However, most systems are not decoupled. So, how do we solve them?

Content:
Let's consider a general linear system of two differential equations:

Content:
[MATH: {x_{1}^{′}(t) = ax_{1}(t) + bx_{2}(t); x_{2}^{′}(t) = cx_{1}(t) + dx_{2}(t)]

Content:
It turns out that if the matrix [MATH: A] has two distinct real eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2], then [MATH: A] is diagonalizable and we can solve the system.

Content:
If the eigenvectors corresponding to [MATH: \color{red}\lambda_1] and [MATH: \color{blue}\lambda_2] are [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},] respectively, then the general solution to our original system can be written as
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
This result is true for any [MATH: n \times n] system with [MATH: n] distinct eigenvalues. We'll prove this result for a [MATH: 2\times 2] system at the end of the lesson.

Content:
Now, let's see some concrete examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding the General Solution Given the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of the Corresponding Matrix

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: [1; − 2]] and [MATH: [2; 5]] be eigenvectors of a matrix [MATH: A] that correspond to eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1=-1] and [MATH: \lambda_2=2,] respectively.
What is the general solution of the matrix differential equation [MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),]
where [MATH: A] has two distinct eigenvalues [MATH: {\color{red}\lambda_1}, {\color{blue}\lambda_2}] with corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},] the formula for the general solution is
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.]

Therefore, the general solution of our matrix differential equation is

[MATH: x(t)|= c_{1}[1; − 2]e^{− t} + c_{2}[2; 5]e^{2t}, c_{1}, c_{2} ∈ R.]
